decisions.title: Transcription of the already-executed Phase 3 User authorization for the .sps/tools attribution-policy migration and the Python unittest CI job
decisions.decision: TWO already-executed, User-authorized changes are transcribed here so that the authorization survives a fresh clone. (1) COMMIT 238c9e4 — '.sps/tools validator migrations + checker/test changes': exactly 6 files are in scope, namely .sps/tools/validate-capability.sh, .sps/tools/validate-control.sh, .sps/tools/validate-governance.sh, sps2/tests/test_attribution_policy.py, sps2/tools/check_p2.py, sps2/tools/check_p3.py. The scope was to migrate the three .sps/tools shell validators onto the canonical attribution policy and to fix checker false-PASS behaviour so that a malformed or unknown input produces a visible non-empty error rather than empty stdout. (2) COMMIT cdcbca8 — 'add Python unittest CI job with a zero-test guard': exactly 1 file is in scope, .github/workflows/sps-ci.yml, adding a fourth CI job named python-unittest alongside the three pre-existing jobs (lint-and-smoke, version-sanity, powershell-syntax), which those three do not alter. The CI scope was to add a job that executes the deterministic Python unittest suite with fetch-depth: 0 and a zero-test guard (RAN == 0 -> fail; RAN < MIN_TESTS=500 -> fail), with no pip install and no network. Both changes were executed before this record was written; this record changes no file and is not authority to change any file.
decisions.reason: The authorization for both commits exists only in reports/SPS2-PHASE3-DECISION-EXECUTION-20261016-082741.md, which is UNTRACKED: 'git ls-files reports/' returns 0 of the 9 report files present on disk. That report is also NOT gitignored (git check-ignore reports/... reports no match), so the loss is not the result of an intentional ignore rule but of the directory never having been added. The consequence recorded as defect DP-10 is that a fresh clone receives both commits in its history while receiving none of the reasoning, scope or authorization that produced them; a future agent would find two commits traceable to no User decision, which is precisely the failure mode .sps/GOVERNANCE.md section 5 exists to prevent ('Prevents future agents from re-litigating settled architecture because they did not know why a decision was made'). Re-stating the authorization in the decision contract makes it durable and machine-checkable. The author is an agent, not a User; under .sps/GOVERNANCE.md the Approval axis is 'User only', so this record can only transcribe an approval that already exists and can never create one.

alternatives.option: Commit reports/ wholesale so the narrative report itself becomes durable
alternatives.why_not_chosen: It makes the evidence durable but leaves it in a non-governance-native form: a fresh clone would gain 9 narrative reports, none of them in the decision contract, none machine-checkable, and the authorization would still not be discoverable by any decision-record consumer. It also expands blast radius from the 2 authorized commits to 9 unrelated files (7 of which record other phases' work), and it does not resolve the governance question of whether an agent-authored narrative may stand as the record of a User approval. Recorded as alternative (a) in the DP-10 trade-off analysis.

alternatives.option: Leave reports/ untracked and treat the two commits as self-documenting via their commit messages
alternatives.why_not_chosen: The commit messages describe what changed, not who authorized it, in what scope, or with what non-goals. Under .sps/GOVERNANCE.md the Approval axis is User-only and must be recorded separately from completion and verification, so a commit message cannot carry the authorization. This is the status quo that produces DP-10.
